lines.text: אח 31 אחד
are used in the same sense for things
feminine, e. g. Ex. 25, 20 וּפְנֵיהֶם אִישׁ
אֶל־אָחִיו and their faces (i. e. of the
Cherubim, shall look) one towards an-
other. 37, 9.
8. Trop. as expressing likeness of dis-
position, habits, etc. Job 30, 29 I am a
brother to jackals, i. e. I cry and howl
like them. Prov. 18, 9.
Deriv. אָחוֹת, אַחֲוָה, and pr. n. אַחְאָב,
אַחְבָּן, אֲחוּמַי, אֲחִי—אֲחִיתֹפֶל.
* II. אָח interj. expressing grief, com-
plaint, onomatopoetic, ah! alas! c. dat.
Ez. 6, 11. 21, 20.—Hence the Arabic verb
أَحْحَاحَ to cry ah, ah, ah! repeatedly;
see below in אָהַהּ.
III. אָח f. Arab. إِخِّ, a large pot, a
portable furnace or stove, in which fire
was kept in the king’s winter-apartment,
Jer. 36, 22. 23. At the present day the
Orientals sometimes make use of such
pots or furnaces instead of fireplaces, for
warming rooms; they are called in Per-
sian and Turkish, تنّور tannûr. They
have the form of a large pitcher; and
are placed in a cavity sunk in the middle
of the apartment. When the fire has
burnt down, a frame like a table is
placed over the pot, and the whole is
then covered with a carpet; and those
who wish to warm themselves sit upon
the floor and thrust their feet and legs
and even the lower part of their bodies
under the carpet. R. אָחַח II.
אַח Chald. a brother; plur. c. suff.
אֶחָיִךְ Ezra 7, 18.
אֹחַ only in plur. אֹחִים, pr. howlings,
shrieks; hence howling animals, doleful
creatures, (comp. אִי II,) prob. howlets,
owls, Is. 13, 21. The word is onomato-
poetic, like Lat. ulula, Germ. Uhu,
Schubut, Fr. hibou. See אָח II, and
r. אָחַח.
אַחְאָב (father’s brother) Ahab, pr. n. m.
a) A king of Israel r. 918—897 B. C.
noted for his uxoriousness and idolatry,
אַחְבָּן (brother of the wise, or for אַחְיָן
brotherly) Ahban, pr. n. of a man of the
tribe of Judah, 1 Chr. 2, 29.
אָחַד a verb derived from the numeral
אֶחָד, not used in Kal, its place being
there supplied by יָחַד to make one, to
unite.
Hithpa. to unite oneself, to collect one-
self. Ez. 21, 21 הִתְאַחֲדִי pr. unite thyself,
[three-edged sword,] i. e. ravage with
all thy force united; or, as the parallel-
ism permits, collect thyself, i. e. attend!—
The suggestion of C. B. Michaelis is not
to be contemned, who regards the four
first words of the verse as spoken in the
character of a military chief: “Conjunge
te, dextrorsum! [aciem] strue, sinis-
trorsum!” i. e. Fall together, right! to
your post, left!
* אֶחָד constr. אַחַד (and so before מִן
Lev. 13, 2; before עָשָׂר Gen. 32, 23;
also Gen. 48, 22. 2 Sam. 17, 22. Zech.
11, 7,) fem. אַחַת for אַחְדַּת, in pause
אֶחָת; a cardinal numeral having the force
of an adjective, one; unus, a, um. Arab.
أَحَدٌ, f. إِحْدَى, Eth. አሐዱ ahadu,
Chald. and Syr. חַד, ܚܰܕ. The same
radical letters are found in the Pehlvi
advek one; and except the third rad.
Daleth, in Sanscr. eka, and Pehlvi jëk.—
32, 30. Josh. 12, 9 sq.—Spec. also
1. one, i. q. the same, Gen. 40, 5. Job
2. As ordinal, the first, primus, a, um,
but only in enumerating the days of the
month. Ezra 10, 16. 17 בְּיוֹם אֶחָד לַחֹדֶשׁ
on the first day of the month. בְּאֶחָד לַחֹדֶשׁ
on the first of the month Gen. 8, 5. 13;
comp. μία τῶν σαββάτων Acts 20, 7. In
enumerating years the construction is
שְׁנַת אַחַת, as sometimes in Engl. the
year one, two, etc. for the first year, Dan.
9, 1. 2. Ezra 1, 1.—In other passages, as
Gen. 1, 5. 2, 11, אֶחָד retains its common
signif. as a cardinal, and the numbers
follow each other as in Engl. one, second,
third; Lat. unus, alter, tertius, Sueton.
Octav. 101.
3. some one, any one, Lev. 13, 2. Deut.
12, 14. 2 Sam. 7, 7. אַחַד הָעָם one of the
people, Gen. 26, 10. 1 Sam. 26, 15.
אֵין אֶחָד, לֹא, no one, Num. 16, 15. 1 K.
8, 56. Ps. 14, 3.—Hence often
4. i. q. the indef. art. a, an, one, espec.
in the later Hebrew. 1 K. 20, 13 נָבִיא

line_status.note: The two readings differ only in item order. In this print the Hebrew items of a list run left-to-right across the line, each followed by its comma (cf. line 3: "pr. n. אַחְאָב,"). Line 4 prints אַחְבָּן, then אֲחוּמַי, then the range אֲחִי—אֲחִיתֹפֶל followed by the period at the far right — continuing the alphabetical sequence after אַחְאָב. Reading A reverses the list. All vowel points (ḥataf-pataḥ under the alephs of אֲחוּמַי and אֲחִי, pataḥ + sheva + dagesh in אַחְבָּן, holem on ת, segol under פ) match B as printed.

The printed Arabic shows a small circle (sukūn) above the first ḥāʾ followed by a separate second ḥāʾ with fatḥa and alif — not a shadda as in Reading A. The exclamation mark and semicolon are also set with a thin space before them, as in B.
The second and third letters are he (open at top-left), not chet, and the final he carries a printed mappiq dot; matches the interjection sense "to cry ah, ah, ah".
The mark above the khā is a w-shaped shadda, not a tanwīn ḍamma, and a kasra is printed beneath the khā; Reading A's إِخِّ matches, Reading B's إِخٌ does not.
Only the shadda is printed over the nūn; no fatḥa on tāʾ and no ḍamma on nūn, so Reading A over-vocalises.
A dot (hireq) is printed under the yod between the qamets of chet and the sheva of final kaf, so the form is אֶחָיִךְ, not אֶחָיךְ.
The third letter of the final word is a short yod (not reaching the baseline like the adjacent vav-height letters), so the printed form is אַחְיָן, as in Reading B; Reading A's vav is wrong.
The second Hebrew word shows shewa under the chet and a patach with dagesh under/in the dalet (אַחְדַּת), not segol–segol as in Reading A.

Under the aleph the print shows a cluster of dots (segol), not a single patach stroke, and under the chet a qamets with its downward tick, not a flat patach. This matches the pausal form אֶחָת that Gesenius gives ("in pause אֶחָת;") just before the definition, so Reading A is correct.
The e of "jek" is printed with a diaeresis (two dots clearly visible above it in the italic word), so "jëk" is correct; Reading A drops the diacritic.
